title: AP Physics C: Mechanics
summary: Use calculus to model motion, forces, energy, momentum, rotation and oscillation.
frameworkNote: Unit map checked against College Board on 15 October 2026 for the 2026-27 course. Each unit has one focused original revision lesson, not exhaustive topic coverage or an official practice paper. Uses the revised seven-unit framework. Gravitation and orbits are integrated into forces and rotating systems; the historical separate gravitation unit is not used.

modules.title: Integrating a changing acceleration
modules.focus: Recover velocity and position with initial conditions.
explanation: Calculus connects position, velocity and acceleration through v=dx/dt and a=dv/dt. Differentiating removes an integration constant; integrating requires an initial condition to recover a particular motion. Keep units consistent in each coefficient.

Area under an acceleration-time curve gives velocity change, while area under velocity gives displacement. Distance travelled uses the integral of |v| and may require splitting at direction changes. Constant-acceleration shortcuts do not apply to a general time-dependent acceleration.

workedExample.prompt: For a(t)=6t m/s² with t in seconds and v(0)=2 m/s, find v(2).
steps: Integrate acceleration to get v(t)=3t²+C; the initial condition gives C=2.

misconception.correction: One integration gives velocity; a second gives position.

questions.prompt: For x(t)=t³-3t in metres, find v at t=2 s.
A particle has v(t)=2t-2 m/s on [0,2] s. Find displacement and distance.
checkpoints: Negative and positive signed areas cancel.

questions.hint: Each integration needs its own constant.
questions.prompt: A particle has a(t)=4t m/s², v(0)=1 m/s and x(0)=0. Find v(2) and x(2).
hints: Each integration needs its own constant.
Use both given initial conditions.

questions.hint: A return to the initial position gives zero average velocity.
questions.prompt: For x(t)=t²−4t metres, compare average velocity on [0,4] s with instantaneous velocity at t=3 s.
questions.answer: Average velocity is [x(4)−x(0)]/4=0. Instantaneous velocity is 2t−4, giving 2 m/s at 3 s.
checkpoints: Use endpoint displacement for the average.
Report the distinct values 0 and 2 m/s.
hints: A return to the initial position gives zero average velocity.
Instantaneous velocity is a local derivative.

notes.title: Reasoning through integrating a changing acceleration
paragraphs: Differentiation and integration connect position, velocity and acceleration, but each operation answers a different question. Differentiating x(t) gives instantaneous velocity and differentiating again gives acceleration. Integrating acceleration gives velocity change, so an initial velocity is still needed to obtain absolute velocity. Integrating velocity gives signed displacement; split the interval at velocity zeros before summing distance. Always check dimensions and initial conditions. A polynomial formula may describe only a stated time interval, and extending it indefinitely can produce motion outside the intended physical model even when the algebra remains defined.

workedExamples.prompt: A particle has v(t)=3t²−6t m/s for 0≤t≤3 s and x(0)=1 m. Find x(3) and distance travelled.
steps: Integrate: x(t)=1+t³−3t². Thus x(3)=1 m and the net displacement is zero.
Velocity changes sign at t=2 s. Positions are x(0)=1, x(2)=−3 and x(3)=1 m, so distance is 4+4=8 m.
workedExamples.conclusion: The final position is 1 m and the distance travelled is 8 m.

flashcards.front: What initial datum is needed after integrating acceleration?
How is instantaneous acceleration obtained from position?
Why split a distance integral at velocity zeros?
flashcards.back: The sign of velocity may change.

flashcards.front: What does ∫v dt give?

modules.title: A resistive force as a differential equation
modules.focus: Model acceleration from the instantaneous velocity.
explanation: Newton’s second law remains a vector equation even when forces depend on time, position or velocity. A linear drag model Fdrag=-bv opposes velocity, with b carrying units kg/s. It is an assumption valid only in an appropriate flow regime.

For vertical falling motion with downward positive, m dv/dt=mg-bv. Terminal velocity occurs when net force vanishes, not when all forces vanish. Initial conditions and the model’s domain determine the particular velocity history.

workedExample.prompt: A falling object has m=2 kg, b=4 kg/s and g=10 m/s². Find terminal downward speed.
steps: At terminal velocity dv/dt=0, so mg=bvterminal.
Thus vterminal=20/4=5 m/s downward.

misconception.claim: Terminal velocity means gravity stops acting.
misconception.correction: Gravity continues but is balanced by the opposing drag force.

questions.prompt: For horizontal motion with only F=-bv, what is the sign of acceleration when v>0?
An object moves in a circular orbit of radius r around mass M. Derive its speed.
questions.hint: Set gravitational force equal to required radial net force.
checkpoints: Cancel m and solve for v.

questions.prompt: For horizontal linear drag with m=3 kg and b=1.5 kg/s, find the time constant and speed fraction after 4 s.
hints: Divide mass by drag coefficient.
Express elapsed time in time constants.

questions.prompt: For downward-positive falling motion m dv/dt=mg−bv, show that vterminal=mg/b is a stable limiting speed.
questions.answer: At v=mg/b the net force is zero. Below it mg−bv>0 accelerates the object downward; above it mg−bv<0 reduces downward speed.
checkpoints: Set acceleration to zero for the terminal value.
Analyse the force sign below it.
Analyse the force sign above it.
hints: Compare drag with weight.
A stable value is approached from either side.

notes.title: Reasoning through a resistive force as a differential equation
paragraphs: A velocity-dependent force turns Newton’s second law into a differential equation. For horizontal linear drag, m dv/dt=−bv, so speed decays exponentially rather than decreasing by equal amounts in equal times. The ratio m/b is a time constant with units of time; after one time constant the velocity is 1/e of its initial value. For vertical falling motion, gravity adds a constant term and the speed approaches a terminal value where net force vanishes. Terminal motion is a dynamic balance of forces, not an absence of either gravity or drag.

workedExamples.prompt: A 2 kg object has horizontal initial speed 8 m/s and linear drag coefficient b=1 kg/s. Find v(t) and displacement by t=2 s.
steps: The equation dv/dt=−v/2 gives v(t)=8e^(−t/2) m/s.
Integrate from 0 to 2: Δx=16(1−e⁻¹) m≈10.1 m.
workedExamples.conclusion: v(t)=8e^(−t/2) m/s and displacement after 2 s is about 10.1 m.

flashcards.front: What is the linear-drag time constant?
What fraction of initial horizontal speed remains after one time constant?
What balances gravity at terminal fall speed?
Does drag cause constant acceleration?
flashcards.back: Not when drag depends on changing velocity.

modules.title: Variable-force work and potential energy
explanation: Work by a variable force is the line integral of force along displacement. In one dimension this becomes the integral of F(x) dx. Net work equals kinetic-energy change regardless of whether the force is constant.

For a conservative force in one dimension, F=-dU/dx. Stable equilibrium occurs at a local minimum of potential energy, where a small displacement produces a restoring force. The zero of potential energy is arbitrary; differences affect the motion.

workedExample.prompt: A force F(x)=4x N, with x in metres, acts from x=0 to x=3 m. Find work.
steps: Integrate 4x to obtain 2x².
Evaluate from 0 to 3: W=18 J.

misconception.claim: The work of a variable force equals its final value times the distance.
misconception.correction: That ignores the force history; integrate or use a justified average.

questions.prompt: For U(x)=3x² J with x in metres, find F at x=2 m.
questions.hint: Differentiate and apply the negative sign.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg particle receives 9 J net work while moving initially at 4 m/s. Find final speed.
questions.hint: Add work to initial kinetic energy.
checkpoints: Final kinetic energy is 25 J, so v²=25.

questions.hint: Force varies with position, so use an integral.
questions.prompt: A force F(x)=6x² N acts from x=1 to x=2 m. Find its work.
hints: Force varies with position, so use an integral.
Subtract the lower-limit antiderivative.

questions.prompt: A particle has total mechanical energy 10 J in a conservative potential with U=12 J at a proposed location. Can it reach that location classically?
questions.answer: No. K=E−U would be −2 J, which is impossible for classical kinetic energy; it must turn before entering that region.
hints: Kinetic energy cannot be negative.
Compare potential energy with the fixed total.

notes.title: Reasoning through variable-force work and potential energy
paragraphs: Work by a variable force is an integral along displacement. In one dimension, a conservative force satisfies F=−dU/dx, so the slope of the potential-energy curve determines force direction. Equilibrium occurs where that slope is zero. A local minimum is stable because small displacements produce forces back towards the minimum; a local maximum is unstable. Adding a constant to U changes its reference without changing forces or energy differences. When using an energy diagram, kinetic energy is E−U, so classically accessible positions require U≤E and turning points occur where kinetic energy becomes zero.

workedExamples.prompt: A particle has potential U(x)=2x²−8x+10 J, with x in metres. Find equilibrium, its stability and work from x=0 to x=3 m.
steps: F=−dU/dx=8−4x N, so equilibrium is x=2 m. U″=4>0 makes it stable.
U(0)=10 J and U(3)=4 J, so conservative work is 10−4=6 J.
workedExamples.conclusion: The stable equilibrium is at 2 m and the force does +6 J of work.

flashcards.front: How is force obtained from U(x)?
What shape of U gives stable equilibrium?
What does E−U represent?
Does adding a constant to U change force?

modules.title: Force-time integration and centre of mass
modules.focus: Apply momentum conservation to the whole system.
explanation: Impulse is the time integral of net force, equal to momentum change. For a variable force, the area of the force-time graph accounts for its full history. Retain direction signs before combining impulses.

The centre of mass follows the external net force according to M acm=Fexternal. Internal forces can redistribute momentum among components without changing total momentum. For explosions or collisions, define the system before deciding which impulse is external.

workedExample.prompt: A force F(t)=6t N acts on a particle from t=0 to 2 s. Find its impulse.
steps: Integrate force: J=integral from 0 to 2 of 6t dt.
The result is [3t²] from 0 to 2=12 N s in the positive direction.

misconception.claim: Internal forces can accelerate an isolated system’s centre of mass.
misconception.correction: Internal action-reaction pairs cancel in the total force; external force controls centre-of-mass acceleration.

questions.prompt: Masses 1 kg and 3 kg lie at x=0 and x=4 m. Find centre-of-mass position.
An initially stationary system separates into 2 kg moving at +3 m/s and 1 kg. Find the second velocity with no external impulse.
checkpoints: The second must have -6 kg m/s.

questions.prompt: Masses 2 kg and 4 kg have velocities +3 m/s and −1 m/s. Find total momentum and centre-of-mass velocity.
hints: Retain the negative velocity.
Divide total momentum by total mass.

questions.hint: Separate overall translation from relative motion.
questions.prompt: An isolated initially stationary pair of masses is pushed apart by an internal spring. Must their centre of mass remain at rest even if their kinetic energy increases?
questions.answer: Yes. External impulse is zero, so total momentum remains zero and vcm=0; spring potential energy can become kinetic energy of relative motion.
checkpoints: Identify spring energy as the kinetic-energy source.
hints: Separate overall translation from relative motion.
Internal energy conversion does not require external impulse.

notes.title: Reasoning through force-time integration and centre of mass
paragraphs: The impulse-momentum theorem applies to time-varying forces by integration. Integrate the external force on the selected system over the interaction interval to find total momentum change. Internal forces can strongly affect individual objects while leaving system momentum unchanged. The centre of mass follows M acm=Fexternal for a constant-mass system, even when its parts move relative to one another. In one dimension, xcm=Σmixi/M and vcm=P/M. These relations help distinguish redistribution inside a system from translation of the system as a whole; kinetic energy can change without changing total momentum.

workedExamples.prompt: A 2 kg particle initially moves at 1 m/s. A net force F(t)=3t² N acts from 0 to 2 s. Find final velocity.
steps: Impulse is ∫₀²3t² dt=[t³]₀²=8 N s.
Initial momentum is 2 kg m/s; final momentum is 10 kg m/s, so vf=10/2=5 m/s.

flashcards.front: What force belongs in a system impulse integral?
How is centre-of-mass velocity related to momentum?
Can internal forces change total system momentum?
What does equal and opposite internal impulse conserve?

modules.title: Moment of inertia from a mass distribution
modules.focus: Integrate distance squared over the object.
explanation: Moment of inertia about an axis is the integral of r² dm. The distance r is perpendicular to the chosen axis. A uniform rod permits dm=(M/L)dx, but a nonuniform density requires a different mass element.

For fixed-axis rotation, net torque equals Iα when I is constant. Changing the axis changes the inertia even though the object stays the same. The parallel-axis theorem I=Icm+Md² connects parallel axes separated by distance d.

workedExample.prompt: Derive the inertia of a uniform thin rod of length L and mass M about an axis perpendicular to one end.
steps: Use dm=(M/L)dx and integrate x² from 0 to L.
I=(M/L)[x³/3] from 0 to L=ML²/3.

misconception.claim: Moment of inertia is an intrinsic number independent of the axis.
misconception.correction: It depends on how mass is distributed relative to the specified axis.

questions.prompt: A rod has M=3 kg and L=2 m. Find its end-axis inertia.
An object has Icm=2 kg m², M=4 kg and a parallel axis 0.5 m away. Find I.

questions.hint: Use the centre of mass as the starting axis.
questions.prompt: A uniform rod has M=6 kg and L=2 m. Use Icm=ML²/12 to find inertia about a parallel axis 1 m from its centre.
hints: Use the centre of mass as the starting axis.
Add rather than subtract the shift term.

questions.hint: All ring mass lies at its radius.
questions.prompt: Two thin rings have equal mass but radii R and 3R. Compare their central-axis inertias and angular accelerations under equal torque.
questions.answer: Ring inertia is MR², so the larger ring has nine times the inertia and one ninth the angular acceleration.
checkpoints: Square the radius factor to obtain nine.
Apply α=τ/I for the inverse acceleration factor.
hints: All ring mass lies at its radius.
Keep torque fixed while changing inertia.

notes.title: Reasoning through moment of inertia from a mass distribution
paragraphs: Moment of inertia is an integral over a mass distribution: I=∫r⊥² dm. The distance is perpendicular to the chosen axis, so changing the axis can change I even for the same object. Choose a mass element suited to the geometry and express dm using a linear, area or volume density. The parallel-axis theorem I=Icm+Md² applies to an axis parallel to one through the centre of mass. It does not replace the need to identify the centre-of-mass axis correctly. Dimensional checks should give mass times length squared, and distant mass contributes disproportionately.

workedExamples.prompt: Derive the inertia of a uniform thin rod of length L and mass M about a perpendicular axis through its centre.
steps: Use x along the rod, dm=(M/L)dx, with limits −L/2 to L/2.
I=(M/L)∫x² dx=(M/L)[x³/3]₋L/₂^L/₂=ML²/12.
workedExamples.conclusion: The centre-axis moment of inertia is ML²/12.

flashcards.front: What distance appears in I=∫r²dm?
flashcards.back: Perpendicular distance to the rotation axis.

flashcards.front: What is dm for a uniform rod element dx?
When can the parallel-axis theorem be used?
flashcards.back: Between parallel axes, one through the centre of mass.

flashcards.front: Why does distant mass matter more?
flashcards.back: Its contribution scales with squared distance.

modules.title: Orbital energy and angular momentum
modules.focus: Use conservation about a specified centre.
explanation: For a particle, angular momentum is r×p. A central force has zero torque about its centre, so angular momentum about that point is conserved. A radial force can still do work when radial motion changes.

For a circular gravitational orbit, K=GMm/(2r) and U=-GMm/r when potential is zero at infinity. Total energy is -GMm/(2r). These circular-orbit expressions should not be inserted unchanged at an arbitrary point of an elliptical trajectory.

workedExample.prompt: A circular orbit radius doubles around the same central mass. Compare orbital speed and total energy.
steps: From v=√(GM/r), speed becomes 1/√2 of its previous value.
From E=-GMm/(2r), energy becomes half its old negative value, so it is less negative.

misconception.claim: Zero torque means no force acts.
misconception.correction: A nonzero radial force can have zero torque about the force centre.

questions.prompt: A spinning object changes I from 6 to 3 kg m² without external torque. Initial ω=2 rad/s. Find final ω.
checkpoints: Initial angular momentum is 12 kg m²/s.

questions.prompt: Why is static friction not necessarily a mechanical-energy loss in ideal rolling on a fixed surface?
questions.answer: With no slipping, that contact point is instantaneously at rest, so ideal static friction there does no work.

questions.prompt: For a circular orbit, radius increases from r to 4r around the same central mass. Compare speed and period.
questions.answer: Speed becomes one half because v∝r⁻¹/²; period becomes eight times because T=2πr/v∝r³/².
checkpoints: Apply the inverse square-root speed scaling.
hints: Use circular orbit assumptions.
The path length grows fourfold while speed halves.

questions.prompt: A satellite in a circular orbit has kinetic energy K. Express its gravitational potential energy and total energy using K.
checkpoints: Relate circular kinetic energy to GMm/r.
hints: Use the circular force balance.
Keep the negative potential-energy sign.

notes.title: Reasoning through orbital energy and angular momentum
paragraphs: A central force exerts zero torque about its force centre, so angular momentum about that centre is conserved. This explains why an orbiting body moves faster near periapsis without requiring constant speed along an elliptical path. For a circular gravitational orbit, inward acceleration gives v²=GM/r, while potential energy with zero at infinity is −GMm/r. Total orbital energy is −GMm/(2r). These circular formulas should not be substituted locally into an elliptical orbit; use energy and angular-momentum conservation with the appropriate orbital conditions instead. A bound orbit has negative total energy in this reference.

workedExamples.prompt: At two points of an orbit, velocity is perpendicular to the radius. At the first r=2R and v=3v₀; at the second r=3R. Find the second speed.
steps: Zero gravitational torque about the central mass conserves L=mrv at these perpendicular points.
m(2R)(3v₀)=m(3R)v₂, so v₂=2v₀.

flashcards.front: Why does gravity conserve angular momentum about the central mass?
flashcards.back: Its force is radial, so torque there is zero.

flashcards.front: What is circular orbital energy?
Can circular-speed formulas be used at every point in an ellipse?
What does negative orbital energy indicate in this model?

modules.title: Differential equations for oscillation
modules.focus: Recognise restoring acceleration proportional to displacement.
explanation: An ideal spring-mass oscillator satisfies d²x/dt²=-(k/m)x. Solutions are sinusoidal, with angular frequency √(k/m). Initial position and velocity set amplitude and phase, so one frequency allows many possible trajectories.

A physical pendulum at small angular displacement obeys approximately Iθ″=-mgdθ, where d is the pivot-to-centre-of-mass distance. Its period is 2π√(I/(mgd)). The small-angle assumption is essential because the exact torque contains sin θ.

workedExample.prompt: For x(t)=0.10 cos(4t) m, find acceleration as a function of time.
steps: Differentiate twice: v=-0.40 sin(4t) m/s and a=-1.60 cos(4t) m/s².
This also equals -16x, consistent with ω²=16 s⁻².

misconception.claim: The small-angle pendulum period formula is exact at every amplitude.
misconception.correction: The linear restoring model approximates sin θ by θ and fails for large amplitudes.

questions.prompt: For k=50 N/m and m=2 kg, find angular frequency.
In x=A cos(ωt), what are position and velocity at t=0?
questions.hint: Evaluate cosine and sine at zero.
Each derivative introduces a factor of two.
questions.prompt: For x(t)=0.30 cos2t m, find v(t), a(t) and maximum speed.
questions.answer: v=−0.60 sin2t m/s; a=−1.20 cos2t m/s²; maximum speed is 0.60 m/s.
checkpoints: Differentiate once with the chain rule.
hints: Each derivative introduces a factor of two.
The sine magnitude cannot exceed one.

questions.prompt: A proposed oscillator solution is x=Ce^(−ωt) for positive ω and nonzero C. Does it solve x″+ω²x=0?
questions.answer: No. Its second derivative is +ω²x, so substitution gives 2ω²x, not zero; it instead solves x″−ω²x=0.
hints: Check the equation directly.
Two differentiations remove the negative exponent coefficient sign.

notes.title: Reasoning through differential equations for oscillation
paragraphs: The equation x″+ω²x=0 describes an ideal linear oscillator, with solutions built from sine and cosine. Initial displacement and initial velocity determine the two integration constants or equivalently the amplitude and phase. Differentiating a proposed solution is the most direct way to verify both the differential equation and the initial conditions. Energy offers a second check: (1/2)mv²+(1/2)kx² should stay constant when damping and external driving are absent. Linear drag changes the equation and gradually removes mechanical energy, so an undamped sinusoid is then only an approximation over an appropriately short interval.

workedExamples.prompt: A mass-spring system has ω=3 rad/s, x(0)=0 and v(0)=0.60 m/s. Find x(t), v(t) and amplitude.
steps: Write x=A cos3t+B sin3t. Initial displacement gives A=0; initial velocity gives 3B=0.60, so B=0.20 m.
Thus x=0.20 sin3t and v=0.60 cos3t; differentiating twice gives x″=−9x.
workedExamples.conclusion: Amplitude is 0.20 m, with x(t)=0.20 sin3t m and v(t)=0.60 cos3t m/s.

flashcards.front: How many initial conditions does x″+ω²x=0 need?
What equation must acceleration satisfy?
What is the amplitude when x(0)=0 and v(0)=v₀?
What does damping do to mechanical energy?
flashcards.back: It transfers energy out of the oscillator’s mechanical store.
